sections.body: This field applies artificial intelligence to the visual and physical planning of live performance. Stage renderings are now produced by image generation models, of which the site tracks 1000 live examples, turning rough sketches into detailed set proposals. Projection mapping uses video models to create moving backdrops that respond to actor positions or script cues. Lighting plots are generated from scene descriptions, and costume synthesis produces fabric patterns and garment shapes before physical samples are made. Acoustic modelling predicts how a set will reflect or absorb sound, helping designers adjust materials early. These tools are in active use by production teams, not just in research papers.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven across the five areas. Stage rendering and costume concept are the most mature, with image generation models producing usable drafts in minutes, though they still require human correction for scale, sightlines and historical accuracy. Projection mapping and generative backdrops work well for abstract or ambient content but struggle with precise alignment on irregular surfaces and real time actor interaction. Lighting plots can be suggested by AI, yet final cue timing and safety checks remain manual. Acoustic modelling is reliable for simple room shapes but less trustworthy for complex sets with moving elements or unusual materials. The honest limit is that no current tool replaces a designer's judgment about how a space feels to an audience.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking for overall set visuals should start with Stage Design and Architectural Rendering, which covers how AI turns a director's notes into buildable drawings. Projection Mapping and Generative Backdrops explains the moving image layer that sits on those surfaces, including the video models behind it. Lighting Plots and Cue Design moves from static set to time based effects, showing how AI proposes light positions and sequences. Costume Concept and Fabric Simulation shifts attention to the performers, using image generation for garment ideas and physics based simulation for drape and movement. Acoustic Modelling for Sets closes the loop by addressing how the built environment shapes sound, which is often overlooked in visual planning. Together these pages follow a production from first sketch to final technical rehearsal.
